title: Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes: understanding a result and planning support
intro: These chromosome conditions affect development before birth and can create lifelong health and support needs. A test result is important information, but it does not describe a child's personality or predict every ability or medical problem. Families deserve clear explanations, time for questions and respectful support with testing, pregnancy decisions and the care of their child.

sections.heading: What the chromosome names mean
paragraphs: Chromosomes carry genetic information. Down syndrome usually involves an extra copy of chromosome 21; Edwards syndrome involves chromosome 18, and Patau syndrome chromosome 13. Sometimes only some cells have the extra material, called mosaicism, or there is a partial extra segment or rearrangement. The exact laboratory result matters for counselling. Most cases arise by chance and are not caused by something a parent ate, felt or did during pregnancy. The chance increases with maternal age, but these conditions can occur at any age. Some rearrangements can be inherited, so a genetics specialist may recommend parental chromosome testing and discuss future pregnancies.

sections.heading: Screening is different from diagnosis
paragraphs: An ultrasound or screening blood test estimates a chance or identifies features that need further assessment. Non-invasive prenatal testing, NIPT, uses a blood sample from the pregnant person and is still screening, even when highly informative. Higher-chance results can be false positives, and lower-chance results do not exclude every condition. Chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis can provide diagnostic chromosome testing, but involve a procedure with risks that need explanation. Ask what the particular test detects, its limitations, timing and whether further clarification could be needed. Screening and diagnostic tests are choices; declining testing should not remove access to ordinary pregnancy care.

sections.heading: Understand the different outlooks without treating them as certainties
paragraphs: People with Down syndrome have varied learning abilities, health needs and levels of independence. Many reach adulthood and participate in education, relationships, work and community life with appropriate support. Heart problems, hearing or vision difficulties and other conditions may need assessment and treatment. Edwards and Patau syndromes often cause serious problems involving several organs, major developmental disability and a high risk of pregnancy loss or early death. Some children live longer, particularly with certain mosaic or partial forms, and each child needs an individual assessment. Neither a chromosome label nor a prenatal scan can precisely predict a particular child's life, development or the family's experience.

sections.heading: Discuss decisions and care with the right team
paragraphs: After a higher-chance or confirmed result, request a clear discussion with maternity or fetal medicine and genetics professionals, with an interpreter if needed. Ask whether the finding is confirmed, what scans show and what remains uncertain. Discuss the options available in your location, including continuing pregnancy, preparing for birth and the options for ending pregnancy where available, without pressure toward one decision. For a continuing pregnancy, plan the place of birth, newborn assessment, feeding, heart and breathing care and the level of treatment appropriate to the child's needs and family goals. Palliative care can support comfort and family time alongside other suitable treatment; it is not abandonment.

sections.heading: Build ongoing support around the person and family
paragraphs: Ask for a named coordinator and a written plan for health checks, early development support, communication, therapies, education and practical assistance. For Down syndrome, hearing, vision and other health surveillance should continue through life rather than assuming every difficulty is part of the condition. For a child with serious illness, discuss symptom relief, feeding help, emergency plans and support at home. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, collapse or a child who is very hard to wake needs emergency care, while new feeding problems or reduced wet nappies need prompt advice. Families may want balanced information from people with lived experience, counselling, respite or bereavement support. Support should recognise different feelings and avoid stereotypes about happiness, burden or what any family must choose.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: clarifying a screening result
examples.text: Amina receives a higher-chance NIPT result. She asks whether this is a diagnosis and arranges counselling about diagnostic testing, its risks and what it could clarify. She includes a support person and interpreter rather than making a major decision from the screening label alone.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: planning individual care
examples.text: After a confirmed diagnosis of Edwards syndrome, a family meets the maternity and children's teams. They discuss the baby's actual findings, possible treatments, comfort, feeding, where birth should take place and how urgent problems will be handled. The plan can be reviewed as new information becomes available.

questions: Is this screening or a confirmed diagnosis, and what does the exact chromosome result mean?
What is known and uncertain about this child's health, and what options are available locally?
Who coordinates medical, developmental, practical and emotional support for us?
